content: Pterygium is a term that typically refers to a benign growth of the conjunctiva, the clear tissue covering the white part of the eye and the inside of the eyelids. It can also describe any wing-like triangular membrane that occurs in other parts of the body, such as the neck, eyelids, knees, elbows, ankles, or fingers. An example of this is popliteal pterygium syndrome, which affects the legs. The word pterygium is derived from the Greek word pterygion, meaning wing. When associated with the conjunctiva, a pterygium most commonly grows from the nasal side of the sclera (the white part of the eye). This growth is thought to be influenced by environmental factors such as sunlight, low humidity, and dust. The predominance of pterygia on the nasal side may be due to the way sunlight passes laterally through the cornea, where it is refracted and focused on the limbal area. Sunlight entering from the lateral side of the eye focuses on the medial limbus after passing through the cornea. On the opposite side, the shadow of the nose reduces the intensity of sunlight focused on the lateral or temporal limbus. The exact time when pterygium was first recognized is unclear. Pterygium can be classified into three main groups based on its characteristics. In the conjunctiva, pterygium is marked by elastic degeneration of collagen and fibrovascular proliferation. It has an advancing portion called the head, which is connected to the main body of the pterygium by the neck. Occasionally, a line of iron deposition, known as Stocker’s line, can be observed adjacent to the head of the pterygium. The location of this line can provide insight into the growth pattern of the pterygium. As a benign growth, pterygium does not require treatment unless it grows to the extent that it covers the pupil and obstructs vision. The exact cause of pterygium is unknown, but it is associated with excessive exposure to wind, sunlight, or sand. Differentiating pterygium from other conditions is important. For example, pinguecula is a degenerative eye condition often confused with pterygium. A pinguecula is a yellowish, slightly raised lesion on the conjunctiva near the limbus. Unlike pterygium, which arises from the limbus and progresses onto the cornea, a pinguecula remains confined to the conjunctiva without involving the cornea. Other conditions that may mimic pterygium include pseudopterygium, carcinoma in situ, squamous cell carcinoma, and other neoplastic diseases. Epidemiological studies have shown that pterygium is more common in older individuals, with the highest prevalence in those over 40 years of age. It is rare in individuals under 20 years old. The incidence is higher in males, occurring approximately twice as frequently as in females. Several risk factors contribute to the development of pterygium, including ultraviolet (UV) light exposure, which can damage cellular DNA, RNA, and extracellular matrix components. Other factors include abnormal conjunctival expression of the tumor suppressor gene p53, angiogenesis-related factors, human papillomavirus (HPV) infection, abnormal human leukocyte antigen (HLA) expression, and a family history of the condition. Routine screening for pterygium is not recommended due to insufficient evidence. The natural history of pterygium is poorly understood. When active, it can grow over months to years, with clinical signs such as redness and localized thickening indicating active inflammation. In its inactive state, pterygium appears white and flat and may remain static for decades without significant growth or clinical impact. It is unclear how pterygium transitions between active and inactive states or whether it can reactivate. Complications of pterygium include distortion or reduction of central vision, redness, irritation, and chronic scarring of the conjunctiva and cornea. Recurrence rates after simple surgical excision to bare sclera are high, ranging from 30% to 80%, and can be as high as 90% in certain populations. This high recurrence rate, even with adjunctive measures, is a major reason why surgery is not recommended for small pterygia, irritation, or cosmetic reasons alone. However, the visual and cosmetic prognosis following pterygium excision is generally good. The procedure is well-tolerated, and most patients can resume normal activities within 48 hours post-surgery. Recurrent pterygia can be treated with repeat surgical excision and grafting, using conjunctival/limbal autografts or amniotic membrane transplants in selected cases. The diagnosis of pterygium is typically made based on its classic clinical appearance as a wedge-shaped growth extending onto the cornea. However, it is important to distinguish pterygium from other conditions with similar appearances, particularly neoplastic lesions. The most common symptoms of pterygium are redness and irritation. Visual impairment is less common. In asymptomatic cases, patients may notice a change in the appearance of their eye, or the pterygium may be incidentally identified during a physical examination. There are no specific laboratory, electrocardiogram (ECG), X-ray, echocardiography, ultrasound, CT scan, or MRI findings associated with pterygium. However, corneal topography can be useful in assessing the degree of irregular astigmatism caused by advanced pterygium. Medical treatment for pterygium is aimed at symptomatic relief and does not halt progression or cause regression of the condition. Patients without vision or eye movement impairment may be treated with topical lubricants such as artificial tears, ointments, or gels, which are available over the counter. Artificial tears are the most commonly used topical lubricant and can help reduce symptoms. They are typically applied one to two drops to the affected area three to four times daily. Preservative-free preparations are recommended for patients with irritation from preservatives or those requiring frequent lubrication, although these are more expensive. Topical decongestants, nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs), and glucocorticoids may also provide symptomatic relief but are associated with adverse effects that limit their use. Topical decongestants can be used to treat redness and irritation not relieved by artificial tears. Definitive treatment for pterygium is achieved only through surgical removal. Long-term follow-up is necessary, as pterygium may recur even after complete surgical correction. Indications for surgical removal include astigmatism causing visual impairment, opacity in the visual axis, documented growth threatening the visual axis, restriction of eye movement, significant cosmetic impact, or intractable irritation. Primary prevention of pterygium involves minimizing UV radiation exposure. Patients are advised to wear hats or caps with brims and use UV-blocking coatings on the lenses of glasses or sunglasses when in areas of sun exposure.
